exercise_group.instructions: Assume that the matrices mentioned in Exercises 1–15 below have appropriate sizes. Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

statement.paragraph: (T/F) If $A$ and $B$ are $m \times n$, then both $A B^{T}$ and $A^{T} B$ are defined.
(T/F) If $A B = C$ and $C$ has $2$ columns, then $A$ has $2$ columns.
(T/F) Left-multiplying a matrix $B$ by a diagonal matrix $A$, with nonzero entries on the diagonal, scales the rows of $B$.﻿
(T/F) If $B C = B D$, then $C = D$.﻿
(T/F) If $AC = 0$, then either $A = 0$ or $C = 0$.﻿
(T/F) If $A$ and $B$ are $n \times n$, then $(A + B)(A - B) = A^{2} - B^{2}$.﻿
(T/F) An elementary $n \times n$ matrix has either $n$ or $n + 1$ nonzero entries.
(T/F) The transpose of an elementary matrix is an elementary matrix.
(T/F) An elementary matrix must be square.
(T/F) Every square matrix is a product of elementary matrices.
(T/F) If $A$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix with three pivot positions, there exist elementary matrices $E_{1},\ldots,E_{p}$ such that $E_{p}\cdots E_{1}A = I$.﻿
(T/F) If $A B = I$, then $A$ is invertible.
(T/F) If $A$ and $B$ are square and invertible, then $A B$ is invertible, and $(A B)^{- 1} = A^{- 1}B^{- 1}$.﻿
(T/F) If $A B = B\mspace{-180mu} A$ and if $A$ is invertible, then $A^{- 1}B = B\mspace{-180mu} A^{- 1}$.﻿
(T/F) If $A$ is invertible and if $r \neq 0$, then $(rA)^{- 1} = rA^{- 1}$.﻿
Find the matrix $C$ whose inverse is $C^{- 1} = \,\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 6 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$.﻿
Let $A = \,\,\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$. Show that $A^{3} = 0$. Use matrix algebra to compute the product $(I - A)(I + A + A^{2})$.﻿
Suppose $A^{n} = 0$ for some $n > 1$. Find an inverse for $I - A$.﻿
Suppose an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ satisfies the equation $A^{2} - 2A + I = 0$. Show that $A^{3} = 3A - 2I$ and $A^{4} = 4A - 3I$.﻿

Let $A = \,\,\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 8 \\ 2 & 4 & {11} \\ 1 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \,\,\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} {- 3} & 5 \\ 1 & 5 \\ 3 & 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack$. Compute $A^{- 1}B$ without computing $A^{- 1}$. [Hint: $A^{- 1}B$ is the solution of the equation $A X = B$.]
Suppose $A B = \,\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 5 & 4 \\ {- 2} & 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$ and $B = \,\begin{bmatrix} 7 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ Find $A$.﻿
Suppose $A$ is invertible. Explain why $A^{T} A$ is also invertible. Then show that $A^{- 1} = (A^{T} A)^{- 1}A^{T}$.﻿
Let $x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$ be fixed numbers. The matrix below, called a Vandermonde matrix, occurs in applications such as signal processing, error-correcting codes, and polynomial interpolation.

Given $\textbf{y} = (y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})$ in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$, suppose $\textbf{c} = (c_{0},\ldots,c_{n - 1})$ in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ satisfies $V\textbf{c} = \textbf{y}\text{,}$ and define the polynomial

list.item: Show that p(x1)=y1,…,p(xn)=yn. We call p(t) an interpolating polynomial for the points (x1,y1),…,(xn,yn) because the graph of p(t) passes through the points.
Suppose x1,…,xn are distinct numbers. Show that the columns of V are linearly independent. [Hint: How many zeros can a polynomial of degree n−1 have?]
Prove: “If x1,…,xn are distinct numbers, and y1,…,yn are arbitrary numbers, then there is an interpolating polynomial of degree ≤n−1 for (x1,y1),…,(xn,yn).”

statement.paragraph: Let $A = L U$, where $L$ is an invertible lower triangular matrix and $U$ is upper triangular. Explain why the first column of $A$ is a multiple of the first column of $L$. How is the second column of $A$ related to the columns of $L$?
Given $\textbf{u}$ in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ with $\textbf{u}^{T}\textbf{u} = 1\text{,}$ let $P = \textbf{uu}^{T}$ (an outer product) and $Q = I - 2P$. Justify statements $(a)$, $(b)$, and $(c)$.

The transformation $\textbf{x}\mapsto\! P\textbf{x}$ is called a projection, and $\textbf{x}\mapsto\! Q\textbf{x}$ is called a Householder reflection. Such reflections are used in computer programs to create multiple zeros in a vector (usually a column of a matrix).

Let $\textbf{u} = \,\,\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\textbf{x} = \,\,\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$. Determine $P$ and $Q$ as in Exercise 27, and compute $P\textbf{x}$ and $Q\textbf{x}$. The figure shows that $Q\textbf{x}$ is the reflection of $\textbf{x}$ through the $x_{1}x_{2}\text{-plane}$.

list.item: A Householder reflection through the plane x3=0.

statement.paragraph: Suppose $C = E_{3}E_{2}E_{1}B$, where $E_{1}$, $E_{2}$, and $E_{3}$ are elementary matrices. Explain why $C$ is row equivalent to $B$.﻿
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ singular matrix. Describe how to construct an $n \times n$ nonzero matrix $B$ such that $A B = 0.$
Let $A$ be a $6 \times 4$ matrix and $B$ a $4 \times 6$ matrix. Show that the $6 \times 6$ matrix $A B$ cannot be invertible.

Suppose $A$ is a $5 \times 3$ matrix and there exists a $3 \times 5$ matrix $C$ such that $C\mspace{-270mu} A = I_{3}$. Suppose further that for some given $\textbf{b}$ in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{5}$, the equation $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$ has at least one solution. Show that this solution is unique.

[T] Certain dynamical systems can be studied by examining powers of a matrix, such as those below. Determine what happens to $A^{k}$ and $B^{k}$ as $k$ increases (for example, try $k = 2,\ldots,16)$. Try to identify what is special about $A$ and $B$. Investigate large powers of other matrices of this type, and make a conjecture about such matrices.

[T] Let $A_{n}$ be the $n \times n$ matrix with $0\text{’s}$ on the main diagonal and $1\text{’s}$ elsewhere. Compute $A_{n}^{- 1}$ for $n = 4\text{,}$ $5$, and $6$, and make a conjecture about the general form of $A_{n}^{- 1}$ for larger values of $n$.﻿
